qs.q:

More students bring reusable water bottles to school now, ______ has reduced plastic waste in the canteen by half.
qs.ex: Ngữ pháp Unit 3 Lớp 12: Đại từ quan hệ 'which' sau dấu phẩy thay thế cho toàn bộ mệnh đề đứng trước.

qs.q: Before putting plastic yoghurt pots into the recycling bin, you should rinse them ______ with water.
qs.ex: Từ vựng Unit 3: rinse out = tráng sạch bên trong hộp/chai trước khi tái chế.

qs.q: Young people today care deeply ______ climate change and plastic pollution in the oceans.
qs.ex: Động từ + giới từ Unit 3: care about = quan tâm đến.

qs.q: Our school has installed automatic sensor taps in all washrooms, ______ helps save thousands of litres of water each month.
qs.ex: Đại từ quan hệ 'which' sau dấu phẩy bổ nghĩa cho cả mệnh đề phía trước.

qs.q: Instead of throwing away fruit peels and vegetable scraps, my mother uses them to make ______ for her garden.
qs.ex: Từ vựng Unit 3: make compost = ủ phân hữu cơ.

qs.q: All the members of our class agreed ______ the plan to ban single-use foam boxes at the school fair.
qs.ex: Động từ + giới từ Unit 3: agree on something (đồng ý về một kế hoạch/vấn đề).

qs.q: Plastic bags take hundreds of years to ______ in landfills, releasing microplastics into the soil.
qs.ex: Từ vựng Unit 3: decompose = phân hủy.

qs.q: Many shoppers still rely ______ convenient single-use plastic bags when buying vegetables at the wet market.
qs.ex: Động từ + giới từ Unit 3: rely on = phụ thuộc vào.

qs.q: My brother forgot to turn off the air conditioner before leaving for school, ______ made my parents very annoyed.
qs.ex: 'which' thay cho toàn bộ sự việc ở mệnh đề trước.

qs.q: If paper boxes are ______ with grease from pizza or fried chicken, they cannot be recycled with clean cardboard.
qs.ex: Từ vựng Unit 3: contaminated = bị bẩn / nhiễm tạp chất dầu mỡ.

qs.q: Thirty students in our grade have applied ______ the position of Green Ambassador this semester.
qs.ex: Động từ + giới từ Unit 3: apply for a position = nộp đơn ứng tuyển vị trí.

qs.q: The teacher explained the rules of sorting waste ______ the students before the clean-up began.
qs.ex: Động từ + giới từ Unit 3: explain something to somebody = giải thích điều gì cho ai.

qs.q: In a compost bin, you should alternate green layers of fruit scraps with brown ______ of dry leaves and shredded paper.
qs.ex: Từ vựng Unit 3 (bài nghe Composting): brown layers of dry leaves = các lớp lá khô màu nâu.

qs.q: We are preparing ______ the school’s Earth Day exhibition by making flowerpots from old plastic bottles.
qs.ex: Động từ + giới từ Unit 3: prepare for = chuẩn bị cho.

qs.q: Supermarkets now sell shampoo and detergent in refillable pouches, ______ cuts down on thick plastic bottles.
qs.ex: 'which' sau dấu phẩy thay cho cả mệnh đề trước.

Taking part in these activities helps young people learn how to reduce plastic packaging sent to landfills and save water and electricity. Educators and families also note that **(3)**______ turn fruit peels and leftovers into nutrient-rich compost for gardens. This month, our organisers **(4)**______ practical workshops on how to practise green living and waste recycling, so please **(5)**______ the activities in your neighbourhood. qs.q:
Mark the letter A, B, C or D on your answer sheet to indicate the best arrangement of utterances or sentences to make a cohesive and coherent exchange or text in each of the following questions from 7 to 11.
**Dear Alex,**
a. At school, our teachers also organise practical projects to help us reduce plastic packaging sent to landfills and save water and electricity.
b. Thank you for your email; it was great to hear about your recent school activities.
c. At weekends, my friends and I join community groups to practise green living and waste recycling at school and at home.
d. I’m writing to tell you about how we are learning about reducing plastic waste, composting leftovers and adopting green living in Unit 3: Green Living.
e. Write back soon and tell me what your school is doing on this topic!
**Best wishes,**
qs.ex: Trình tự bức thư: Cảm ơn thư trước (b) → Nêu lý do viết thư chia sẻ chủ đề Unit (d) → Kể hoạt động ở trường (a) → Kể hoạt động cuối tuần (c) → Lời kết thư (e): b - d - a - c - e.

qs.q:
a. Nam: Yes, definitely! Let’s sign up together after class today.
b. Mai: Nam, our school club is holding a workshop on reducing plastic waste, composting leftovers and adopting green living this Saturday. Would you like to join?
c. Mai: Great! I’ll get two registration forms from the club leader.
qs.ex: Trình tự hội thoại 3 lượt: Mai rủ Nam tham gia workshop chủ đề Unit (b) → Nam đồng ý đăng ký (a) → Mai nói sẽ đi lấy phiếu đăng ký (c): b - a - c.

qs.q:
a. To address this, schools and communities are now launching new green-living habits at school and at home.

**PERSPECTIVES ON GREEN LIVING**
In recent years, reducing plastic waste, composting leftovers and adopting green living has attracted growing attention from educators and researchers alike. A recent national survey reports that while over eighty per cent of students and households recognise the importance of green-living habits, only about thirty-five per cent have <u>**recycled**</u> these practices into their daily routines at school and at home. Even when resources are available, many people still struggle to balance their busy schedules with the need to practise green living and waste recycling.
The challenge lies not only in awareness but also in daily habits. Researchers note that active participants regularly engage in structured tasks that reduce plastic packaging sent to landfills and save water and electricity, whereas passive observers only join occasional events once or twice a year. Consistent practice requires patience and planning, but it delivers lasting rewards. Many individuals simply repeat outdated habits they observed in the past, which prevents them from experiencing how green-living habits can turn fruit peels and leftovers into nutrient-rich compost for gardens.
Fortunately, attitudes are shifting rapidly. **[I]** Most respondents in the survey agreed that everyone should practise green living and waste recycling, even though many admitted spending less than two hours a week on it themselves. **[II]** Progress was strongest in communities where schools and families worked together as partners. **[III]** Groups can begin by setting clear weekly goals and giving every member a practical role at school and at home. **[IV]** Small, steady steps like these can turn a difficult challenge into a shared habit of cooperation.
Promoting reducing plastic waste, composting leftovers and adopting green living matters for the long-term future. Young people who see students and households model positive behaviours are likely to view these practices as normal, and <u>**they**</u> will carry those values into adulthood. In this way, green-living habits not only reduce plastic packaging sent to landfills and save water and electricity today but also turn fruit peels and leftovers into nutrient-rich compost for gardens for generations to come.
(Adapted from Educational & Social Research Reports – Unit 3: Green Living)

**PERSPECTIVES ON GREEN LIVING**
In recent years, reducing plastic waste, composting leftovers and adopting green living has attracted growing attention from educators and researchers alike. A recent national survey reports that while over eighty per cent of students and households recognise the importance of green-living habits, only about thirty-five per cent have <u>**recycled**</u> these practices into their daily routines at school and at home. Even when resources are available, many people still struggle to balance their busy schedules with the need to practise green living and waste recycling.
The challenge lies not only in awareness but also in daily habits. Researchers note that active participants regularly engage in structured tasks that reduce plastic packaging sent to landfills and save water and electricity, whereas passive observers only join occasional events once or twice a year. Consistent practice requires patience and planning, but it delivers lasting rewards. Many individuals simply repeat outdated habits they observed in the past, which prevents them from experiencing how green-living habits can turn fruit peels and leftovers into nutrient-rich compost for gardens.
Fortunately, attitudes are shifting rapidly. **[I]** Most respondents in the survey agreed that everyone should practise green living and waste recycling, even though many admitted spending less than two hours a week on it themselves. **[II]** Progress was strongest in communities where schools and families worked together as partners. **[III]** Groups can begin by setting clear weekly goals and giving every member a practical role at school and at home. **[IV]** Small, steady steps like these can turn a difficult challenge into a shared habit of cooperation.
Promoting reducing plastic waste, composting leftovers and adopting green living matters for the long-term future. Young people who see students and households model positive behaviours are likely to view these practices as normal, and <u>**they**</u> will carry those values into adulthood. In this way, green-living habits not only reduce plastic packaging sent to landfills and save water and electricity today but also turn fruit peels and leftovers into nutrient-rich compost for gardens for generations to come.

**MAKING GREEN LIVING PART OF DAILY LIFE**
Taking time to practise green living and waste recycling may seem ordinary at first glance, yet a growing body of research highlights its transformative power. Studies show that well-designed green-living habits help students and households reduce plastic packaging sent to landfills and save water and electricity. At the same time, these practices turn fruit peels and leftovers into nutrient-rich compost for gardens and foster stronger cooperation at school and at home.
Despite these clear advantages, participation in green-living habits has faced obstacles in recent years. Researchers report that <u>**they**</u> have been neglected in many busy communities due to modern time pressures. <u>**Tight timetables, heavy workloads and a lack of practical guidance can all prevent people from maintaining positive routines.**</u> Even when individuals want to improve, distractions often get in the way.
The encouraging news is that success does not require perfection from day one. Experts emphasise that building <u>**reusable**</u> habits is about steady progress rather than instant results. Students and households can start with simple steps at school and at home, share responsibilities and use practical checklists to stay on track. Those who understand the purpose behind reducing plastic waste, composting leftovers and adopting green living become much more resilient and motivated.
Of course, no single workshop or rule will solve every challenge overnight, and some groups need time to adapt. That is no reason to give up. Even one or two focused sessions a week can spark meaningful change, and the positive <u>**container**</u> will grow stronger over time. What matters most is the commitment people bring to supporting one another every day.
(Adapted from Global Success Reading Series – Unit 3: Green Living)

**PARTNERSHIPS BETWEEN SCHOOLS AND FAMILIES IN UNIT 3: GREEN LIVING**
Over the past two years, a research team from the National Institute of Education has tracked 1,500 high school students to evaluate how reducing plastic waste, composting leftovers and adopting green living affects teenager development. The study found that while nearly ninety per cent of students and households valued green-living habits, only forty-two per cent <u>**sustained**</u> these routines throughout the entire school year. Students who tried to practise alone often gave up after a few weeks when exam pressure increased.
By contrast, learners whose families and teachers coordinated their guidance achieved far more durable results. In households where parents actively joined weekend activities to practise green living and waste recycling at school and at home, teenagers were twice as likely to reduce plastic packaging sent to landfills and save water and electricity. Researchers explained that shared routines reduce the feeling of isolation and turn abstract classroom advice into enjoyable daily habits. Moreover, consistent family involvement helps turn fruit peels and leftovers into nutrient-rich compost for gardens without adding extra stress to students’ timetables.
Schools across the country are now redesigning their programmes based on these findings. **[I]** Instead of assigning theoretical worksheets, teachers invite parents and students to co-sign a simple weekly action plan. **[II]** This joint commitment ensures that classroom lessons are reinforced at home every evening. **[III]** At monthly review sessions, classes celebrate collective progress and exchange practical solutions to common obstacles. **[IV]**
The long-term implications of this partnership model are encouraging. When students and households work side by side, <u>**they**</u> build mutual respect and lasting life skills. Ultimately, integrating reducing plastic waste, composting leftovers and adopting green living into both school curricula and family life prepares young citizens to thrive in an increasingly complex world.
(Adapted from National Educational Research Reports – Unit 3: Green Living)

**WHY CONSISTENCY MATTERS MORE THAN PERFECTION IN UNIT 3: GREEN LIVING**
When people first decide to focus on reducing plastic waste, composting leftovers and adopting green living, they often set overly ambitious targets. Enthusiastic beginners might promise to transform their entire lifestyle in a single weekend, only to feel exhausted a few days later. Studies on habit formation show that well-paced green-living habits are far more effective when built step by step, helping students and households reduce plastic packaging sent to landfills and save water and electricity without burnout.
The main reason crash campaigns fail is that <u>**they**</u> demand too much willpower at once. <u>**Small, consistent efforts practised every day produce far more lasting results than occasional bursts of intense activity.**</u> When a routine fits naturally into a family’s or student’s daily schedule, it requires less mental strain to maintain.
Experts therefore recommend a <u>**gradual**</u> approach to practise green living and waste recycling at school and at home. By starting with one simple task each day and celebrating weekly milestones, learners steadily build momentum. Such steady practice not only strengthens personal discipline but also helps communities turn fruit peels and leftovers into nutrient-rich compost for gardens.
Of course, occasional setbacks are normal during busy exam weeks or family events. Rather than abandoning the goal altogether, resilient learners simply resume their routine the next morning, knowing that patience will <u>**foster**</u> long-term success.
(Adapted from Global Success Reading Series – Unit 3: Green Living)

**COMMUNITY ACTION AND PEER MENTORING IN UNIT 3: GREEN LIVING**
Last year, youth unions in three provinces launched a six-month pilot programme to promote reducing plastic waste, composting leftovers and adopting green living at the grassroots level. Instead of relying on formal lectures, organisers trained two hundred high school volunteers to lead weekend activities where neighbours could practise green living and waste recycling at school and at home. Within the first two months, local communities reported <u>**tangible**</u> improvements in daily habits and neighbourhood solidarity.
A key factor behind this success was peer-to-peer mentoring. Teenagers often feel intimidated when adults lecture them, but they respond enthusiastically when classmates demonstrate how green-living habits can reduce plastic packaging sent to landfills and save water and electricity. By working in small teams of five or six, participants shared practical tips, solved everyday problems together and helped one another turn fruit peels and leftovers into nutrient-rich compost for gardens.
Organisers also introduced simple tools to keep momentum high. **[I]** Every participating household received a visual progress board to track weekly milestones. **[II]** Local cultural centres hosted monthly gatherings where teams showcased their most creative ideas. **[III]** These celebrations turned routine tasks into a source of shared pride across the entire district. **[IV]**
Follow-up surveys conducted six months later confirmed that over seventy-five per cent of participants continued practising green-living habits independently. When student volunteers take ownership of community initiatives, <u>**their**</u> enthusiasm inspires both younger children and older residents. The pilot programme demonstrates that youth-led action is one of the most powerful ways to bring the values of Unit 3: Green Living to life.
(Adapted from Community Development & Youth Studies – Unit 3: Green Living)

**THE RIPPLE EFFECT OF PEER LEADERSHIP IN UNIT 3: GREEN LIVING**
How do positive habits spread across a school or neighbourhood? Sociologists studying reducing plastic waste, composting leftovers and adopting green living have discovered that peer influence is often stronger than formal rules. When students and households see their close friends willingly engage in green-living habits, they are far more likely to join in and reduce plastic packaging sent to landfills and save water and electricity.
Nevertheless, launching a new initiative is never without challenges. Organisers note that initial doubts and busy routines are common, and <u>**they**</u> can slow down participation during the first week. <u>**Young people learn most effectively when they observe respected peers applying positive habits in real-life situations.**</u>
For this reason, many schools encourage <u>**voluntary**</u> student ambassadors to lead by example. Whether demonstrating how to practise green living and waste recycling at school and at home or sharing practical tips during break time, these role models create a welcoming ripple effect that helps the whole school turn fruit peels and leftovers into nutrient-rich compost for gardens.
Even when a minor <u>**obstacle**</u> arises, a supportive peer group keeps members motivated. What begins as the effort of a few enthusiastic students soon grows into a proud tradition shared by the entire community.
(Adapted from Global Success Reading Series – Unit 3: Green Living)

**Read the passage and mark the letter A, B, C or D on your answer sheet to indicate the best answer to each of the following questions from 17 to 26.**

**OVERCOMING BARRIERS TO DAILY PRACTICE IN UNIT 3: GREEN LIVING**
Why do many high school students agree that reducing plastic waste, composting leftovers and adopting green living is important, yet still find it difficult to practise green living and waste recycling at school and at home every day? Educational psychologists point out that modern teenagers face three main barriers: digital distractions, academic pressure and a lack of structured routines. When students feel overwhelmed, they often become <u>**reluctant**</u> to take on new responsibilities at home or in the community.
Fortunately, behavioural research shows that breaking large goals into micro-habits can overcome this hesitation. Instead of trying to change everything overnight, students and households can start with a fifteen-minute daily routine focused on green-living habits. These manageable actions quickly build confidence and help learners reduce plastic packaging sent to landfills and save water and electricity without interfering with their homework.
Another effective strategy is using a structured weekly checklist. **[I]** When teenagers write down specific times and places for their tasks, they are three times more likely to follow through. **[II]** Sharing <u>**it**</u> with a supportive classmate or family member adds friendly accountability. **[III]** Rather than feeling pressured, students enjoy tracking their streak of completed tasks and seeing how their efforts turn fruit peels and leftovers into nutrient-rich compost for gardens. **[IV]**
Teachers who have introduced micro-habits and checklists into their lessons on Unit 3: Green Living report remarkable improvements in student engagement. Once young people realise that small daily choices lead to meaningful results, green-living habits stops feeling like a burden and becomes a natural part of who they are.
(Adapted from Adolescent Psychology & Education Review – Unit 3: Green Living)

qs.ex: reluctant = ngần ngại, miễn cưỡng (hesitant and unwilling).

Ultimately, blending modern convenience with timeless values helps communities <u>**enhance**</u> their daily routines and turn fruit peels and leftovers into nutrient-rich compost for gardens in a sustainable way.

**EXPERIENTIAL LEARNING AND THE FUTURE OF UNIT 3: GREEN LIVING**
Across Viet Nam, forward-thinking high schools are transforming how students learn about reducing plastic waste, composting leftovers and adopting green living. Rather than treating Unit 3: Green Living as a set of vocabulary items to memorise for a test, teachers are integrating experiential learning into every week of the semester. Educators agree that hands-on practice is <u>**indispensable**</u> if young people are to reduce plastic packaging sent to landfills and save water and electricity.
In these classrooms, students work in project teams to investigate real issues and propose ways to practise green living and waste recycling at school and at home. For instance, learners might interview local residents, design bilingual awareness posters or organise a school-wide campaign on green-living habits. Through these authentic tasks, students and households discover how their classroom English connects directly to everyday life.
Assessment methods are evolving alongside teaching styles. **[I]** Instead of relying solely on written quizzes, schools evaluate how effectively students collaborate and apply their plans. **[II]** Each team keeps a reflective portfolio documenting the challenges they faced and how their actions helped turn fruit peels and leftovers into nutrient-rich compost for gardens. **[III]** This approach rewards creativity, persistence and genuine teamwork rather than rote memorisation. **[IV]**
Graduates of experiential programmes consistently report higher confidence when entering university and the workplace. Students <u>**who**</u> have practised solving real-world problems in high school adapt much faster to new environments. By making reducing plastic waste, composting leftovers and adopting green living an active, lived experience, education equips the next generation with both language proficiency and civic responsibility.
(Adapted from Modern Curriculum & Pedagogy Journal – Unit 3: Green Living)

**EXPERIENTIAL LEARNING AND THE FUTURE OF UNIT 3: GREEN LIVING**
Across Viet Nam, forward-thinking high schools are transforming how students learn about reducing plastic waste, composting leftovers and adopting green living. Rather than treating Unit 3: Green Living as a set of vocabulary items to memorise for a test, teachers are integrating experiential learning into every week of the semester. Educators agree that hands-on practice is <u>**indispensable**</u> if young people are to reduce plastic packaging sent to landfills and save water and electricity.
In these classrooms, students work in project teams to investigate real issues and propose ways to practise green living and waste recycling at school and at home. For instance, learners might interview local residents, design bilingual awareness posters or organise a school-wide campaign on green-living habits. Through these authentic tasks, students and households discover how their classroom English connects directly to everyday life.
Assessment methods are evolving alongside teaching styles. **[I]** Instead of relying solely on written quizzes, schools evaluate how effectively students collaborate and apply their plans. **[II]** Each team keeps a reflective portfolio documenting the challenges they faced and how their actions helped turn fruit peels and leftovers into nutrient-rich compost for gardens. **[III]** This approach rewards creativity, persistence and genuine teamwork rather than rote memorisation. **[IV]**
Graduates of experiential programmes consistently report higher confidence when entering university and the workplace. Students <u>**who**</u> have practised solving real-world problems in high school adapt much faster to new environments. By making reducing plastic waste, composting leftovers and adopting green living an active, lived experience, education equips the next generation with both language proficiency and civic responsibility.
(Adapted from Modern Curriculum & Pedagogy Journal – Unit 3: Green Living)

**SELF-REFLECTION AND LONG-TERM GROWTH IN UNIT 3: GREEN LIVING**
Practising green-living habits is even more rewarding when learners take a few minutes each week to reflect on their progress. Educators studying reducing plastic waste, composting leftovers and adopting green living have found that students who keep a brief weekly journal understand their own habits much better and find it easier to reduce plastic packaging sent to landfills and save water and electricity.
During busy weeks, people sometimes miss a planned task or make mistakes. Without reflection, <u>**they**</u> may feel discouraged and assume that their efforts have failed. <u>**Honest self-reflection allows learners to turn early mistakes into valuable lessons rather than reasons to give up.**</u>
To make reflection effective, teachers recommend asking <u>**constructive**</u> questions every Sunday evening: What went well when we tried to practise green living and waste recycling at school and at home this week, and what small adjustment will help us improve next week?
Over time, this simple habit deepens personal <u>**commitment**</u> and helps students and households turn fruit peels and leftovers into nutrient-rich compost for gardens with confidence and pride.
(Adapted from Global Success Reading Series – Unit 3: Green Living)

It replaces all English examinations at the end of the term.
It allows students to skip all weekend activities.
It requires learners to write fifty pages every night.
